title: Chapter 18: Networking, HTTP, and JSON Boundaries
description: Specify process boundaries that remain correct under partial reads, malformed data, slow peers, and dependency failure. Learners frame TCP messages, apply HTTP method and status semantics, use Java HttpClient with deadlines, validate bounded JSON DTOs, and combine idempotency, retry classification, exponential backoff, jitter, circuit breaking, and concurrency isolation responsibly.

lessons.title: TCP sockets, byte-stream framing, timeouts, limits, and cleanup

exercises.title: TCP sockets, byte-stream framing, timeouts, limits, and cleanup: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Can one TCP read be assumed to contain one complete application message?
choices: No; framing and partial-read handling are required
Yes; every write is preserved as a read
hints: Consider what happens when a peer's single write is larger than a network buffer, and why one socket read is not guaranteed to match one application write.

exercises.title: Chapter 18 implementation lab: retryDelay
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `retryDelay`. Return exponential delay min(1000 * 2^attempt, 30000); treat negative attempts as zero. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Clamp negative attempts to zero and cap at 30000 before a shift could overflow. All int attempts are permitted.
hints: Clamp the attempt count itself (for example to 5) before shifting, so the shift amount cannot overflow before the min() cap applies.
Treat negative attempts as zero before computing 1000 << attempt, then cap the result at 30000.

exercises.title: Inspect status before treating a response as success
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the supplied defect so the program writes exactly `ERROR`. The status check currently treats any code under 500 as success, which misclassifies a client error like 404; preserve the branching structure while correcting which status range counts as success, and explain why your fix changes the result instead of hard-coding the print. Output tests verify the printed result; preserving the intended status classification requires reading the source, not just matching output.
hints: This contract recognizes only 2xx as success, not every non-5xx response.

exercises.title: Portfolio checkpoint: idempotent quiz scorer
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Implement QuizScorer.run(String input) as the pure decision core behind the Online Quiz Platform project. Each nonblank trimmed line is one command; blank lines are skipped and produce no output line. DEFINE|quizId|answers registers a quiz (quizId matching [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,20}, not already defined) whose answers is a comma-separated list of 1 to 20 letters, each exactly A, B, C, or D; prints OK or ERROR. SUBMIT|quizId|attemptId|answers requires quizId to be defined, the submitted answers to have the same count as the quiz's defined answers with every letter in A-D, and attemptId to match the same id pattern. If this is the first submission for this exact (quizId, attemptId) pair, compute the score as the count of positions where the submitted answer matches the defined correct answer, record it, and print SCORE|<score>. If (quizId, attemptId) was already submitted with the identical answers, print DUPLICATE|<score> using the originally recorded score, without rescoring. If it was already submitted with different answers, print CONFLICT without changing the recorded result. A malformed submission (wrong quizId, wrong answer count, or an invalid letter) prints ERROR. Output is one line per nonblank input line, joined with \n, no trailing newline. This models only the scoring-and-idempotency core; a real platform's authentication and leaderboard are external, ungraded scope.
hints: attemptId uniqueness for scoring purposes is scoped per quizId, not global — the same attemptId could in principle be reused on a different quiz.
Compare the identical-versus-different answers check exactly (same list, same order) before deciding DUPLICATE versus CONFLICT.
